title: Handling Errors (Advanced)
description: Advanced: read error messages, catch errors with try and except, and raise your own.

subLevels.title: Reading error messages
subLevels.summary: Understand tracebacks and the most common error types.

blocks.text: When Python meets a line it can't run, it stops and prints an error message. Errors that happen while a program runs are called exceptions. Every programmer sees them every day: they are clues, not failures.

blocks.output:
Start
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(10 / 0)
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
explanation: Line 1 runs and prints Start.
Line 2 can't be done, so Python stops and shows the error.
Line 3 never runs: nothing after an error runs.

items: An exception stops the program at the line where it happens.
Everything printed before the error stays on the screen.
The lines after the error do not run.

blocks.text: The message Python prints is called a traceback. Read it from the bottom up.

items: Traceback (most recent call last): Python is about to show where it was.
File "main.py", line 2: the line number where the error happened.
The next line repeats the code from that line.
Under that, Python 3.11 may add a row of ^ or ~ marks pointing at the exact part that failed (left out in these lessons).
The last line gives the error type and a short message. Read this first.

blocks.text: Read a traceback from the bottom: the last line says what went wrong, the line number says where.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: In the Practical tab your program is always called main.py, so tracebacks point to main.py.
Three errors you will meet a lot. Each example shows only the last line of the error.

explanation: NameError: the name was never created, or it is spelled differently.
blocks.caption: Only the last line of the error is shown.

blocks.output: TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
explanation: TypeError: the values are the wrong types for this job, here text + a number.
blocks.caption: Only the last line of the error is shown.

blocks.output: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'ten'
explanation: ValueError: the type is right (a string), but this value can't be converted.
blocks.caption: Only the last line of the error is shown.

explanation: ZeroDivisionError: dividing by zero is impossible.
blocks.caption: Only the last line of the error is shown.

blocks.output: IndexError: list index out of range
explanation: IndexError: the list has positions 0 and 1 only.
blocks.caption: Only the last line of the error is shown.

explanation: KeyError: the dictionary has no key called milk.
blocks.caption: Only the last line of the error is shown.

blocks.text: The error type on the last line already tells you what kind of problem to look for.

items: NameError: unknown name
TypeError: wrong type for the job
ValueError: right type, bad value
ZeroDivisionError: divided by zero
IndexError: list position doesn't exist
KeyError: dictionary key doesn't exist

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Every error type in this level is also in the Glossary, if you need a reminder.
To fix an error: read the last line, go to the line number, and look at the part that is underlined. Here the variable was created as total but used as totl.

blocks.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(totl)
NameError: name 'totl' is not defined
explanation: Line 2 uses totl; changing it to total fixes the program.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Reading only the top of the traceback. The useful part is at the bottom: the error type and message. Also, the line number is where Python noticed the problem; sometimes the real mistake is earlier, like a name spelled differently when it was created.

questions.prompt: Which error does this code cause?
questions.explanation: total exists, but totl was never created, so Python doesn't know that name: NameError.
questions.hint: Compare the name that was created with the name that is printed, letter by letter.
optionFeedback: A TypeError is about mixing the wrong types; here the name itself is unknown.
A ValueError needs a value that can't be converted; no conversion happens here.
A KeyError comes from a missing dictionary key; there is no dictionary here.
Right: totl is a name Python has never seen.

questions.prompt: In a traceback, which line tells you the type of error?
options: The first line, Traceback (most recent call last):
The line that starts with File "main.py"
questions.explanation: The last line shows the error type and its message, such as ZeroDivisionError: division by zero.
questions.hint: Remember which direction the lesson said you should read a traceback from.
optionFeedback: Right: the error type and message are always at the bottom.
The first line only says a traceback is starting; it never names the error.
The File line tells you where the error happened, not what kind it is.
The ^ marks underline the part of the code; the error type is printed below them.

questions.prompt: What does line 3 mean in File "main.py", line 3, in <module>?
options: The error happened on line 3 of main.py
questions.explanation: The File line points to the line Python was running when the error happened.
questions.hint: Think about what a traceback needs to tell you so you can find the problem.
optionFeedback: The number says where the error is, not how long the program is.
Python stops at the first error, so a traceback describes just one error.
Right: it is the line number where Python stopped.
Only the line named in the traceback is where Python stopped.

questions.prompt: Which error does this code cause?
questions.explanation: int() gets a string, which is the right type, but "5.5" is not a whole number, so the value is bad.
questions.hint: int() accepts strings, so ask yourself whether this particular string can become a whole number.
optionFeedback: int() is happy to take a string, so the type is not the problem.
Right: the type is fine but this value can't become an int.
Every name here exists: int and number are both fine.
There is no division anywhere in this line.

questions.prompt: Which error does this code cause?
questions.explanation: marks has only the key "maths", so looking up "english" raises a KeyError.
questions.hint: Look at what kind of collection marks is and what is being looked up.
optionFeedback: IndexError is for list positions; marks is a dictionary looked up by key.
marks is a name that exists; it is the key inside it that is missing.
Right: the dictionary has no english key.
No text is being converted to a number here.

questions.prompt: Which error does this code cause?
questions.explanation: + can join two strings or add two numbers, but not a string and an int: TypeError.
questions.hint: Check the types of the two values on each side of the plus sign.
optionFeedback: Nothing is being converted with int(); the problem is mixing two types.
Right: text and a number can't be joined with +.
There are no variable names here at all, only values.
This line adds, it doesn't divide.

questions.prompt: What appears on the screen?
options: A and B, then the error message
A, the error message, then B
questions.explanation: print("A") runs first. The division by zero stops the program, so print("B") never runs.
questions.hint: Python runs lines in order and stops for good at the first error.
optionFeedback: Right: A is printed, then the program stops at line 2.
Line 1 runs before the error, so A is already on the screen.
B would come after the error, and nothing runs after an error.
The program doesn't continue after the error, so B is never printed.

subLevels.title: try and except
subLevels.summary: Catch an error and keep the program running.

blocks.text: Put code that might fail inside a try block. If an error happens there, Python jumps to the except block instead of stopping the program.

blocks.output:
That was not a number
Program keeps going
explanation: int("abc") raises a ValueError, so Python jumps straight to except.
"Converted!" is skipped because it comes after the error inside try.
After the except block, the program carries on as normal.

items: try: the code that might fail.
except ErrorType: what to do if that error happens.
If the try block has no error, the except block is skipped.

blocks.text: Write the error type after except, so you only catch the problem you expect. You can have several except blocks, one per error type.

blocks.output:
book
5 is too big
two is not a number
explanation: "1" works: items[1] is book.
"5" converts, but there is no position 5: IndexError.
"two" can't be converted: ValueError.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: If no except block matches the error, it is not caught and the program stops as usual.
except: with no error type catches every error, even your own typos. Here "42" is a fine number, but valeu is misspelt, and the message hides the real NameError.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Writing except: with no error type. It catches every error, including spelling mistakes, and shows the wrong message. Name the error you expect, like except ValueError:.
Keep try blocks small and catch the specific error you expect.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: print("A") runs, then int("hi") fails, so print("B") is skipped and the except block prints C.
questions.hint: Follow the try block line by line and notice exactly where the jump happens.
optionFeedback: B comes after the failing line inside try, so it is skipped.
print("A") runs before the error, so A is printed first.
The ValueError is caught, so the except block runs and prints C.
Right: A prints, the error skips B, and except prints C.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: int("7") works, so the try block finishes and the except block is skipped.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything inside the try block actually fails here.
optionFeedback: "7" is a valid whole number, so there is no ValueError to catch.
except only runs when an error happens, and here nothing fails.
Right: no error happens, so except is skipped.
x is the number 7 after int(), so + 1 does maths, not joining text.

questions.prompt: Which word goes in the blank to catch a division by zero?
questions.explanation: Dividing by zero raises ZeroDivisionError, so that is the type to name after except.
questions.hint: Use the exact name Python prints on the last line when you divide by zero.
optionFeedback: A ValueError is for bad values like int("abc"); dividing by zero has its own error type.
Right: that is the exact name of the error.
Python has no error called DivideError; the name must match exactly.
Close, but the real name is longer; error names must be spelled exactly.

questions.prompt: Which statement is true?
options: If no except block matches the error, the program still stops with that error
The except block runs every time, even with no error
Python goes back and runs the try block again
Lines after the error inside try still run
questions.explanation: except only catches the error types it names. Any other error stops the program as usual.
questions.hint: Think about an except ValueError block meeting a completely different kind of error.
optionFeedback: Right: an error with no matching except is not caught.
except only runs when a matching error happens in the try block.
Python never repeats the try block by itself; it moves on.
As soon as an error happens, the rest of the try block is skipped.

questions.prompt: Why does this print "Please type a number" even though "42" is a number?
options: except: catches every error, including the NameError from the typo valeu
print() is not allowed inside try
questions.explanation: valeu was never created, so line 3 raises a NameError. The bare except: catches it and shows a misleading message.
questions.hint: Look closely at the spelling of every name inside the try block.
optionFeedback: Right: the bare except: hides a NameError.
"42" converts to 42 without any problem.
Any code, including print(), can go inside a try block.
Using a name that doesn't exist is a NameError, not a ValueError.

subLevels.title: else, finally and raise
subLevels.summary: Run code after success, always clean up, and raise your own errors.

blocks.text: An else block after except runs only if the try block finished with no error.

explanation: int("25") works, so except is skipped and else runs.
Keeping only the risky line in try makes it clear what you are protecting.

items: try: the risky line.
except: runs if that error happens.
else: runs if no error happened.

blocks.output:
2.0
Done
Cannot divide by zero
Done
explanation: finally runs after try works and after an error is caught: every time.

blocks.text: Order: try, then except (if there was an error) or else (if there wasn't), then finally (always).
raise creates an error on purpose, with your own message. Use it when a value breaks your rules. It stops the function, just like a normal error.

blocks.caption: Only the last line of the error is shown.

blocks.text: The code that calls the function can catch it. except ValueError as error: also stores the error, and printing it shows the message.

blocks.output: TypeError: exceptions must derive from BaseException
blocks.caption: Only the last line of the error is shown.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Raising plain text, like raise "Too big". raise needs an error type with the message in brackets: raise ValueError("Too big").

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: int("4") works, so except is skipped and else prints 4 * 2.
questions.hint: Decide first whether the try block raised an error, then pick the block that runs.
optionFeedback: "4" converts fine, so the except block is skipped.
Right: no error, so else runs and prints 8.
except and else never both run for the same try.
n is the number 4 after int(), so * 2 is maths, not repeating text.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The division fails, so except prints oops; finally always runs afterwards and prints end.
questions.hint: Work out which blocks run when there is an error, and in what order.
optionFeedback: The error is caught, so the except block also runs before finally.
finally runs every time, even after an error was caught.
Right: except runs first, then finally.
finally runs last, after the except block.

questions.prompt: When does the else block of a try statement run?
options: Only when the try block finished with no error
Only when there is no except block
questions.explanation: else is the success path: it runs when try had no error.
questions.hint: Think of else as the opposite path to except.
optionFeedback: Right: else is for when everything worked.
That describes except; else is for the opposite case.
finally is the block that runs every time, and it runs last.
In this lesson else comes after an except block; it runs when try succeeds.

questions.prompt: Which word fills the blank to create an error with your own message?
questions.explanation: raise ValueError("...") creates an error on purpose and stops the function.
questions.hint: This is the keyword from the lesson that creates an error on purpose.
optionFeedback: Right: raise creates the error.
Some other languages use throw, but Python does not have that keyword.
return gives back a value normally; it doesn't create an error.
except catches errors; it doesn't create them.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: check(50) raises ValueError("too big"). except ... as e catches it, and printing e shows its message.
questions.hint: Check whether 50 breaks the rule, and remember what printing the stored error shows.
optionFeedback: 50 is bigger than 10, so raise runs before return.
The except block prints "Error:" before the message.
Printing the error shows its message, not the name of its type.
Right: the error is caught and its message is printed.

questions.prompt: Why does this give a TypeError instead of showing the message?
options: raise only works inside a try block
raise needs an error type, like raise ValueError("Out of stock")
raise must be followed by finally
questions.explanation: You can only raise errors, not plain text. Put the message inside an error type.
questions.hint: Look at what comes straight after the keyword and compare it with the lesson.
optionFeedback: raise works anywhere, inside or outside try.
Right: raise needs an error type, not plain text.
Single and double quotes make the same string; the quotes are not the issue.
finally belongs to try statements; raise doesn't need it.

subLevels.title: Checking input in a loop
subLevels.summary: Keep asking until the user types something valid.

blocks.text: Users make typos. Combine while True, try/except and break to keep asking until the answer is valid.

blocks.output:
Enter your age: abc
Please type a whole number.
Enter your age: -5
Age can't be negative.
Enter your age: 18
Thanks! Age: 18
explanation: abc can't be converted: the except block prints a message and continue asks again.
-5 converts, but it breaks the rule, so the loop asks again.
18 is valid, so break ends the loop.

items: while True: keep asking.
try/except: catch answers that aren't numbers.
if: check your own rules.
break: stop once the answer is valid.

blocks.text: Put the loop in a function. return ends the loop and gives back the valid number. raise inside try sends rule-breaking numbers to the same except block.

blocks.output:
How many tickets (1-6)? seven
Please type a whole number from 1 to 6.
How many tickets (1-6)? 9
Please type a whole number from 1 to 6.
How many tickets (1-6)? 2
Booked 2 tickets

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Converting the input above the try block, like age = int(input("Age: ")) on its own line. A bad answer then crashes the program before try is reached. The line that can fail must be inside try.
Validation loop: ask, try to convert, check your rules, and only leave the loop with a valid value.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: "x" fails to convert, "-2" breaks the rule, and "7" is valid, so it prints ok 7 and break stops the loop.
questions.hint: Walk through the three answers one at a time and note what each one prints.
optionFeedback: Right: each of the three answers prints one line.
"x" and "-2" come first and each prints a message before 7 is reached.
"-2" converts to a number, but it is below 0, so it prints negative.
"7" is valid, so the loop prints ok 7 before break ends it.

questions.prompt: Typing abc here still crashes the program. Why?
options: int(input(...)) is above the try block, so its ValueError is not caught
print() can't be used inside try
input() always crashes when letters are typed
questions.explanation: Only errors that happen inside try are caught. The conversion happens before try starts.
questions.hint: Find the exact line that fails when letters are typed, and check where it is.
optionFeedback: int("abc") raises a ValueError, so ValueError is the right type to catch.
Right: the failing line must be inside try.
print() is fine inside try; the problem is on the line above it.
input() happily returns letters; it is int() that fails.

questions.prompt: Which word goes in the blank so the loop asks again after a bad answer?
questions.explanation: continue jumps back to the top of the loop, which asks the question again.
questions.hint: You need the loop keyword that skips the rest and starts the next round.
optionFeedback: break would leave the loop even though no valid number was typed.
This code is not inside a function, so return can't be used here.
Right: continue goes back to the question.
finally starts a block of a try statement; it doesn't send the loop back.

cheatSheet.title: Handling Errors

items.note: TypeError: wrong types for the job.
ValueError: right type, value can't be used.
ZeroDivisionError, IndexError and KeyError: no such number, position or key.
else: no error happened. finally: always runs.
raise an error with your own message.

remember: Read a traceback from the bottom.
Keep only the risky line inside try.
